title: Studios reverse engineering games with AI and trying to cash in on "copyslop"
author: jimbo-slim
selftext:
I had a feeling this was coming.

After seeing a post on twitter suggesting that the most recent models (Opus 5+, Astra, etc.) were able to effectively reverse engineer entire games from just the binary files, I had to try for myself. Turns out this is entirely possible. I gave Opus 5 access to a game I bought on steam, and within an hour had access to every line of code, asset, animation, you name it, from the entire game. 

Fast forward a few days. I see a paid ad on Instagram for a new friendslop style game, How to Hunt. It looks almost exactly like How to Fish, the most recent viral friendslop success. See for yourself:

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5208540/How\_to\_Hunt/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5208540/How_to_Hunt/)

for reference, How to Fish: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4001890/How\_to\_Fish/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4001890/How_to_Fish/)

At first I assumed that this was from the same dev, but it isn't. This Lazy Turtle Games studio has only to this point released what seem like low effort games, I can see the free character and asset packs on the cover art.

I can only conclude that Lazy Turtle Games bought a copy of How to Fish, had a model reverse engineer it, added a few new animals and are now trying to cash in on an almost complete copy. Watch the trailer. Exactly the same down to the same art style, font and popup when you shoot an animal as in how to fish. the people look the same, the hand setup, etc. 

What are the implications of this? Do you think Lazy Turtle can actually publish such an obvious copy? Does copyright law have anything to say about this?

Ps1 bios 
The games rom 
Psxi emulator (probing) 
Cmake 
Python 

And just a 
orchestration.md file 
Research.md 
Agent_workflow.md 

Clean folder to work in 
folder to place godot game in 
Folder where it does smoke tests 
Folder to test extraction tests 
And just let it do it's thing 

It will build it's own set of additional .MD documents 
And automate the process in phases 

When orchestrator reaches 400k+- contexts 
You let it update handover.md

replies.author: nexisforge
replies.body:
The way LLMs work by pattern matching and predicting what is the next token. When you throw at them obfuscate code that throws them into a much larger guessing game, it becomes very expansive guessing game. The most important part is that will produce very unreliable results, basically deeply broken code. 
Not every obfuscation is the same, some scramble logic, inject fake functionality. 
If a game is shipped with just plain build you don't really need AI, you can decompile it and have the code human readable, then you can start replacing art, renaming UIs, basically a a blatant copy.
If you want to prevent this and make financially impossible for the thieve, you add two levels of protection. Some code runs on the server and is never shipped to the client, AI can't hack into your server and steal that code, that code can also be obfuscated. The encryption of the data on the wire doesn't mean and help in anyway unless you pass passwords. AI can't break that, if it can then the entire internet is broken. And one the when we have quantum compute and they can crack these algorithms then we'll use the same computers to create new ones. So let's leave this aside.

Then why not everyone have obfuscation an server side component in their games. 
Obfuscation can and it will introduce bugs, your game can be broken silently, so you have to manually test the final build. Then some fields have to be omitted from the obfuscation, JSON mapping to classes for example,  so now you have to manually exclude those. AI can definitely help here but for sure you'll have to retest all of it

The server. So players now need internet to play your single player game. And you have to manage servers, I know free ir cheap version, I know all that, but it's a consideration. Depending on what the role of the server is, now you have to write that code that is not shipped with your game.

Bottom line, go with obfuscation and server if you really want to protect your game, amd if your game prject is a super low effort that can be decompiled in a few seconds, assets can be replaced that it will be. These thieves will create and already pipelines to do that and it's only going to get worse.

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body:
Although copying has always been a thing, I can see it becoming a bigger issue. 

Previously, as a game developer, you could assume players had no incentive to play a sloppy copy because they usually wanted the best version of what they wanted to play, not the cheapest (their time and attention are not endless). And you would usually still have the best version, because the other rogue developer had to catch up to you - if you continue development, they are always lagging behind. 

But now you don't have a head start of years or months, but just weeks, maybe even days, depending on the size of the game.

And for us using AI to develop, this is going to be especially critical, because the stuff you produce with AI can't be copyrighted, or at the very least, it will be hard to defend legally.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Depends. If you do no hands on work, then your ability to sue for copyright is limited, although there are still cases to be made for thousands of prompts that it takes to put together the composition for a game. The individual assets are not protected, but if they're used in anything even remotely similar they would be, as someone would be stealing the composition. If, on the other hand, you also manually create or do large amounts of edits to assets, those will be individually copyrighted. That includes 3d gens. So for instance, if I gen a character from Tripo but have to rebuild a chunk of the mesh, the original character that was produced is not copyrighted, but the one that you edited and rebuilt (and frankly most every single character being pushed out of Tripo should have a minimum amount of work done with it, at least currently)  IS protected in full.

Hell if you generate in parts like is recommended, and then merge them together into a single fbx for your character, it's now fully protected, even if you didn't touch a vertice. So it's not particularly hard to copyright individual parts of your game. Doesn't help with a Chinese company coming in and ripping the whole thing off though, as copyright is only protected so far as it is enforced.

comments.author: IkuraNugget
comments.body:
I do see this as a problem but not as big as a problem as we may be catastrophizing.

What I mean by that is we just need to see some actual unprecedented legal cases make headway with lawsuits. Once the risk outweighs the reward less people will be afraid of copying games straight out the box.

But yea until that happens though it will be a problem. Having said that I do think that copying something and reskinning it is still not enough to steal sales. 

The original game will still be the thing gamers flock to, not the knock offs. You might be able to steal sales but it’s the same concept as buying a Gucci bag versus a knock-off Gucci bag. Or a Rolex versus a fake Rolex.

Point is, if your game has gone viral already, you won’t be losing much sales from copycats. There’s also a marketing problem that copycats have to solve.

The only real danger I think is if copycats copy before your game goes viral and also has a means to market their game, then they may potentially steal your vitality. 

In that situation though you have more grounds for a lawsuit, but I get it. It’s still a headache to deal with and costs money to fight those lawsuits. 

The point I’m making though is, because of all of these factors I do expect to see copycats but not that many successful ones. Which is less catastrophic than the idea that this will change “game dev meta” and foster a new wave of rampant copycats.

comments.author: Ok-Way-9449
comments.body:
I had a JAVA emulator of Tera Online MMO years ago. I set it up played and figured out how to give my character anything I wanted. It was fun but I wanted to be able to create a new quest. I asked around and the skills required were way over my head.  A few years later along comes AI and lo and behold I asked how it was done in the game and it explained it to me. Anything that was server side I could edit and change easily. But the quest NPC text was in the client and wasn't Java. It took me playing around and I finally got the client unpacked once I got hold of the keys for that client version. It was an early alpha version that someone got a hold of that created the emulator many years ago. The next problem was repacking, and it just kept failing. I was impressed at how hard it tried to solve the problem. I took the problem and asked a couple other AI about it took their answers and fed it back to my AI and wala, problem solved. I soon learned that every time you had a major accomplishment in my reverse engineering that the AI would not have any idea what it had done in the past. Once I started tasking the AI to create a document that any other AI could use to do what we just finished doing that problem went away by telling it to read the document before proceeding. I was able to fix every quest on the Island of Dawn that was broken and even eventually was able to add in the missing dungeon. It was a fun way to learn about AI.

I am currently working on a game using the play style of one game with classes from another. Every time I have made good progress, I look at what I have say that's not quite what I want and start over with lessons learned. I an on my 4th iteration and I have gone from making sprites and animating them to a paperdoll rigging and cutouts of the characters.   
  
What I love is the adventure you go through with AI creating your game and what you learn along the way.

replies.author: PLYoung
replies.body:
It depends on the game engine and language(s) used.

Games made in Unity and Godot for example uses C# (gdscript also in Godot's case) for your game code and the exe is just a pre-compiled engine template. You do not need the exe's code, you want the decompiled C# or gdscript.  
  
A C# DLLs can very easily be decompiled since they include a lot of information - it being byte code based language. Gdscript is interpreted language so there is no binary and this can be extracted from the data package file.

replies.author: PLYoung
replies.body:
I must have had tunnel vision or they changed it since last I checked. Anyway, there we have it then. Made it Unity.

On the code side it should be quite easy to decompile if the developers did not use IL2CPP since it is just dotnot binaries (not native binaries). There are tools to do it, like ILSpy. 

On the assets side there are tools like Asset Ripper that can extract it.

So, getting the code and assets has been possible long before LLMs came along.

What I am curious about is how opus went about it. What was your setup like during the test? Did you give opus access to the internet to grab the tools it can use in the task? If not ,then its training data must include info about how this can be done - ex, trained on the source code of tools like these since they are open source.
